A collage is a work of art — or any composition — made by taking separate, pre-existing pieces of material and sticking them together onto a flat surface to create one unified whole.

The word names both the process and the finished result. So the thing you make is a collage, and the activity of making it is also called collaging (or making a collage).

The materials used can be almost anything flat enough to be glued down:

  • Cut or torn pieces of newspaper or magazine pages
  • Photographs (printed or cut from magazines)
  • Colored paper, wrapping paper, tissue paper
  • Fabric scraps, ribbons, or thread
  • Receipts, tickets, labels, or other everyday paper items
  • Paint or drawn marks added on top of the pasted pieces

The defining feature is this: you did not create those pieces from scratch. You took things that already existed — a photo, a page from an old book, a scrap of cloth — and arranged them together to make something new. That act of combining ready-made fragments is what makes something a collage.

Think of it like building a picture using puzzle pieces — except you choose the pieces yourself, cut them into whatever shapes you want, and arrange them in any order you like. Usually, the pieces are glued or pasted onto a background (a sheet of paper, a canvas, a board).

Here's what's special: the individual pieces often remain visible and recognizable. If you paste a photograph of a face onto a collage, the viewer can still see it's a photograph. If you paste a strip of newspaper, they can likely read some of the words. The collage doesn't hide its ingredients — it celebrates them.

Because a collage brings together fragments from very different sources, it often creates a feeling of richness, layering, and complexity. Two things that normally have nothing to do with each other — say, a photo of the moon and a piece of floral fabric — can be placed side by side to create a surprising or beautiful effect.

This is one of the reasons collage became so popular in art: it lets you create meaning through contrast and combination, not just through drawing skill.

The word "collage" appears in many areas beyond traditional paper-and-glue art:

In visual art: This is the original and most common use. Artists cut and paste physical materials to make collages. The great Spanish artist Pablo Picasso was among the first to use collage seriously in fine art, in the early 1900s.

In photography (photo collage): Multiple photographs are arranged and combined — either physically printed and stuck together, or digitally on a computer — to make a single image. A photo collage of someone's birthday, for example, might contain 20 different photos arranged in a grid or overlapping pattern.

In digital art: Using software like Photoshop, artists create collages by layering digital images, textures, and graphics. The principle is exactly the same — combining separate elements — just done on a screen instead of a table.

In music: A musical collage is a piece made by blending together sound samples, fragments of other recordings, or very different musical styles. Hip-hop production, for instance, often works like a collage: the producer takes short samples from many old songs and combines them into something new.

In film and video: A video collage (sometimes called a montage) is made by cutting together footage, images, and sounds from different sources to create a new audiovisual experience.

Beyond art, "collage" is often used figuratively to describe anything that is made up of many different, varied pieces coming together:

"The film is a collage of his childhood memories."
"The city's culture is a collage of immigrant traditions."
"Her speech was a collage of quotes, personal stories, and statistics."

In these cases, the speaker means that the thing in question is rich, varied, and assembled from many different sources — just like a real collage. It's not literally made of paper and glue, but the idea of assembling unlike fragments into a whole applies perfectly.
How Collage Differs From Related Things

It helps to know what a collage is not, to sharpen the picture:

  • A painting or drawing is created from scratch using paint, pencil, or ink. A collage uses pre-existing materials. (You can add paint to a collage, though — many collages mix both.)
  • A mosaic is made from small pieces of stone, tile, or glass, usually set into cement or grout. It's related in spirit (combining fragments), but it's three-dimensional and uses hard materials.
  • An assemblage is like a collage, but three-dimensional — objects are arranged and fixed together in space, not just on a flat surface. A collage is essentially a flat assemblage.
  • A montage (especially in film) refers specifically to the technique of editing together a rapid sequence of images or scenes. The words "collage" and "montage" overlap and are sometimes used interchangeably in everyday speech, but "montage" leans more toward film and sequence, while "collage" leans toward visual art and simultaneity.

A collage is a composition — most often a work of art — made by assembling and adhering fragments of pre-existing materials (paper, photos, fabric, etc.) onto a surface to form a new unified whole. The magic of a collage lies in the fact that its parts come from different places and different lives, yet together they create something coherent, surprising, or beautiful. By extension, the word is used in any field — music, film, writing, everyday language — to describe something built from many varied, combined elements.
